title: Gentle pitch and counting
purpose: Try a slightly higher, comfortable pitch on a hum, then keep it while you count, without losing the bright, forward sound.
instructions: Warm up with a few easy glides up and down.
Hum a few times at your everyday speaking pitch, with your tongue forward and a small smile, as in the forward hum.
Now hum a little higher than that: a small, smooth step, not a leap.
Keep that hum and open it into counting, one to five, then breathe normally. Repeat a few times.
When five feels easy, try counting to twenty.

primary_cue.text: Just a little higher than usual, still bright and forward.

cues.text: Just a little higher than usual, still bright and forward.
Go back to the forward hum at your usual pitch until it's bright again, then step up only a little.

practice_task.prompt_text: Hum a little higher than usual, then count: one, two, three, four, five.

check_questions.text: Could you keep the slightly higher pitch and the bright, forward sound while you counted?
Did it sound like you, or like a cartoon voice?

dose_guidance.text: No set number: a few unhurried rounds. Finding a new pitch takes time and concentration, so go easy on yourself.

expected_observations: If a higher pitch sounds cartoon-like, the resonance is often staying dark. That's why the forward hum comes first.
common_misunderstandings: Pitch is one part of a voice, not the whole goal, and no number shows whether your voice sounds the way you want.
Higher isn't automatically better. Pick a comfortable level that sounds like you.
stop_conditions: Anything hurts, feels tight or scratchy, or your voice turns hoarse: that usually means too much, too soon.
Rest your voice and come back another day, starting smaller.

Hoarseness that lasts more than about three weeks, sudden voice loss or pain needs a GP or primary care doctor, who can have your vocal folds looked at. A speech and language therapist who works with voices can help with technique.
adaptations: Stay with counting to five for as long as you need.
limitations: Written for Lilt for practising on your own. Lilt can't check your technique, and it doesn't replace a speech and language therapist.
Lilt shows pitch to describe a take. It isn't validated for coaching and never sets a target for you.

Version 3 (2026-11-08) matched the stop sign for lasting hoarseness to the course (a GP or primary care doctor first, who can have your vocal folds looked at) and described the hum by the tongue and smile, not a buzz to chase, since a buzz isn't resonance. Keeps the earlier versions' questions, answers and cues so coaching works the same. No clinician has reviewed it.
